headline: India removes over 130 million names from voter lists

sources.title: Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi detained over election chief protest (Al Jazeera)
India opposition leader detained during protest against election chief (AP, via La Nación)
India opposition leaders briefly detained in election protest (AFP, via The Star)

chunks.text: Police in New Delhi [[detained]] Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi on October 7, 2026. It was the third time in two days. He and other opposition lawmakers were marching toward a [[protest site]] in the capital. On October 6, police {{broke up}} a march from parliament and {{let the lawmakers go}} soon after. Gandhi said the protesters {{showed up}} again [[without warning]]. They are {{calling for}} India's chief election commissioner to {{step down}}.

verbs.correct: To make a crowd leave a place
verbs.wrong: To count the people in a crowd
verbs.why: Police often break up crowds outside the stadium after a game. Teachers break up large groups in the hallway between classes. On October 6, police broke up a march from parliament.
Police often ask a driver a few questions and then let him go. A store sometimes lets a young shoplifter go after a warning. Police let the lawmakers go soon after the march on October 6.
Only a few people show up for early morning meetings. A friend sometimes shows up at my door with a cake. Gandhi said the protesters showed up again without warning.

verbs.correct: To say that something must happen
verbs.wrong: To vote against a new law
verbs.why: Parents call for safer roads near the school. Workers call for higher pay when prices rise. The protesters are calling for the chief election commissioner to resign.
Many coaches step down at the end of a bad season. A mayor sometimes steps down after a scandal. The protesters want India's chief election commissioner to step down.

chunks.text: The protests are about a huge [[revision]] of India's [[voter lists]]. The Election Commission began {{carrying it out}} in one eastern state in 2025. It has since spread to most of the country's other states. According to the Associated Press, more than 130 million names have been {{taken off}} the lists. Millions of people have [[appealed]] the [[removals]]. About 969 million people were [[eligible]] to vote in India's 2024 election.

verbs.correct: To do a planned piece of work
verbs.wrong: To pay for a large project
verbs.why: The city carries out repairs on its bridges every spring. Nurses carry out tests on every new patient. The Election Commission began carrying out the revision in one state in 2025.

verbs.correct: To remove something from a list
verbs.wrong: To print a list on paper
verbs.why: A hotel takes your name off the list when you cancel. Stores take old phones off their websites when new models arrive. More than 130 million names have been taken off India's voter lists.

chunks.text: Opposition parties say many [[legitimate]] voters have been {{left out}}. They claim the changes [[unfairly]] removed more people who support the opposition. Some critics say [[minority groups]] have been hurt the most, especially Muslims. The opposition wants the revision stopped and the names {{put back}} on the lists. In September, an Indian newspaper reported that two of the commission's three members had [[objected]] at least 14 times to [[key decisions]].

verbs.wrong: To move someone to a new city
verbs.why: Some team photos leave out players who arrive late. A careless clerk sometimes leaves names out of an official list. Opposition parties say many legitimate voters have been left out.

verbs.correct: To return something to its place
verbs.wrong: To print something in a newspaper
verbs.why: Careful shoppers put items back on the shelf when they change their minds. A good cook puts the milk back in the fridge right away. The opposition wants the removed names put back on the voter lists.

chunks.text: The commission and Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party deny any [[wrongdoing]]. The commission says the revision aims to {{weed out}} [[duplicate]] and ineligible names. It says it is {{cracking down on}} [[fake registrations]] while keeping eligible voters on the lists. India's Supreme Court has ordered the government and the commission to explain decisions linked to the revision. Another [[hearing]] was expected in mid-October.

verbs.correct: To find and remove what is not wanted
verbs.wrong: To print names in large letters
verbs.why: The company weeds out weak job applicants early. Good editors weed out mistakes before a book goes to print. The commission says the revision aims to weed out duplicate names.

verbs.correct: To act strongly to stop something
verbs.wrong: To keep a secret about something
verbs.why: The city cracks down on drivers who park illegally. Schools crack down on cheating during exams. The commission says it is cracking down on fake registrations.

mainIdea.s: India's main opposition leader was held by police during protests over a huge change to voter lists. Over 130 million names were removed, and critics fear many real voters were dropped.
mainIdea.why: Opposition parties say many legitimate voters have been left out. More than 130 million names have been taken off the lists.

mainIdea.s: Indian police detained a top opposition figure after a court found that millions of voters had been deleted by mistake. Judges have now told election officials to restore every missing name.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the Supreme Court has only ordered officials to explain their decisions. The opposition, not the court, wants the names put back.

mainIdea.s: India's election body plans to open thousands of new polling stations in small villages. Officials hope shorter lines will help more young people cast a ballot in the next national vote.
mainIdea.why: Protests are growing over a voter list revision. More than 130 million names have been taken off the lists, and the opposition is calling for change.

tf.s: Opposition parties say no legitimate voters have been left out.
tf.why: Opposition parties say many legitimate voters have been left out of the lists.

tf.s: The protesters are calling for the prime minister to step down.
tf.why: They want India's chief election commissioner to step down, not the prime minister.

tf.s: The commission says the revision aims to weed out duplicate names.
tf.why: It says it wants to remove duplicate and ineligible names and keep eligible voters on the lists.

lines.text: Did you see the news from India? Rahul Gandhi was detained again.
He and other lawmakers were marching in New Delhi. They're {{calling for}} the chief election commissioner to {{step down}}.
Why are they so angry at him?
It's about a huge review of the voter lists. More than 130 million names have been {{taken off}}.
130 million? There's [[a lot at stake]] here.
The review started in one state in 2025. Now they're {{carrying it out}} in most of the country.
And the opposition thinks real voters got {{left out}}?
Yes. Millions of people have appealed, and the opposition wants the names {{put back}}.
What does the Election Commission say?
It says it's trying to {{weed out}} duplicate names and {{crack down on}} fake ones.
[[That's the thing]]. Both sides say they're protecting voters.
Right. There are [[two sides to every story]].
Does the Supreme Court have any role?
It has ordered the government and the commission to explain their decisions.
So [[it's not over yet]]. Did the police {{let the protesters go}}?
After the first march, yes. But they {{showed up}} again the next day, and the police {{broke up}} that one too.
Wow. I'll [[keep an eye on]] this story.
